newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Language of peoples' struggle from Kabila No. 2.
newsitem.headline: Language of peoples' struggle from Kabila No. 2.

text.p: Elections will be held in the new Democratic Republic of Congo only after Zaire's people have been re-educated, starting at the level of peasant collectives, a senior aide to Laurent Kabila said on Monday.

In an ideological statement constructed like an epic poem and redolent of the rhetoric of 1960s anti-colonialism, Deogratias Bugera said elections would be transparent and open to all, but they were only a means to an end.
"Be patient," he said when asked for a date.

Kabila is under heavy pressure from world powers to move speedily from military victory over the dictatorial regime of ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko to a pluralist democracy embracing all political currents in the country.
Bugera said it could be "three days, five days or a week" before the new, self-declared president of the renamed state would arrive in the capital, Kinshasa.
Kabila is currently headquartered in Lubumbashi in the extreme southeast of the country, a much smaller city which is nevertheless constantly rumoured to be a potential new capital.

Bugera's statement, read to journalists at the renamed Voice of Congo radio station and broadcast to the people, was puncuated with the repeated refrain: "Dear compatriots, dear comrades of the struggle".
It had the "year zero" tone of many historical revolutionary declarations made in the aftermath of toppling a long-standing dictatorship.
Kabila's victorious rebels Congo had won a "David and Goliath" struggle against the Mobutu regime.

He was a deeply corrupt leader who profited cynically from the "spirit of submission and servility" instilled in the people by rapacious European colonists to exploit his own people for the benefit of himself and a small clique, it said.
The psychological legacy of Mobutu's 32 years of political exclusion of the masses would have to be corrected before a meaningful process of democratisation could succeed, Bugera said.
"We must reawaken the population politically. It is our first duty."

Political training would start at the level of peasants and villagers, or "the collectivity", said Bugera, who is secretary general of the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo, and who was introduced as the "number two personality" in the movement.

"The aim is to avoid the possibility in the future that any one man can confiscate power," he said. To ensure that, Kabila's movement intended to create genuine autonomy at all levels of society, from the peasants up.
In the meantime, the new rulers of the republic would keep their promise to proceed directly to the formation of a constituent assembly which would thrash out a transitional constitution.
There was no suggestion in the statement of Kabila establishing a communist state. Autonomy included economic independence and free enterprise, Bugera said.
In recent statements in Lubumbashi, the rebel alliance made clear it intends to create a market economy and to encourage foreign investment on an attractive, profit-making basis.
But true to Kabila's revolutionary roots in the liberation struggles of the late 1950s and early 60s, Bugera's statement was replete with the proud and bitter rhetoric of decolonisation.
